title: The Banach Fixed-Point Theorem
subject: Real Analysis
statement: A contraction mapping on a complete metric space has exactly one fixed point, and repeated iteration reaches it from any starting point.
short: Completeness plus a Lipschitz constant strictly below 1 forces a unique solution that ordinary iteration finds.
long: A contraction shrinks every distance by a uniform factor c < 1. Because the ambient space is complete, the Cauchy sequence of successive iterates actually converges to a point inside the space. That limit is forced to be a fixed point, and two fixed points cannot coexist because their distance would have to be at most c times itself.
proof: d(x_{n+1},x_n) \le c^n d(x_1,x_0), so the iterates form a Cauchy sequence. Completeness gives x_n \to x^*; continuity of T gives T x^*=x^*. If x^*,y^* are fixed then d(x^*,y^*) \le c\,d(x^*,y^*), hence the distance is zero.
consequence: It gives constructive existence and uniqueness for ODEs (Picard iteration), many numerical root-finding schemes, and the self-similarity theory behind fractals.

title: The Extreme Value Theorem
subject: Real Analysis
statement: A continuous function on a closed bounded interval attains its maximum and minimum.
short: Continuity alone is not enough; compactness of the domain is what guarantees the extremes are achieved.
long: On an open interval the function 1/x has no maximum, and on the bounded open interval (0,1) it is unbounded. Adding the endpoints changes everything: a continuous image of a compact set is compact, hence closed and bounded, so the supremum and infimum are actually values of the function.
proof: A continuous image of a compact set is compact. In the real line compact sets are closed and bounded, so sup f and inf f belong to f([a,b]).
consequence: This is the workhorse behind the existence of best approximations, optimisation on compact domains, and the proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra via minimisation.

title: The Intermediate Value Theorem
subject: Real Analysis
statement: A continuous real function takes every value between any two of its values.
short: The graph of a continuous function on an interval cannot jump over a horizontal line.
long: The result looks obvious when drawn, but it depends on the least upper bound property of the real numbers. Over the rationals it fails: a continuous rational-valued function can change sign without ever taking the value zero.
proof: Let S={x\in[a,b]: f(x)\le y} and c=\sup S. Continuity forces f(c)=y; otherwise a small neighbourhood of c would contradict the definition of supremum.
consequence: It proves the existence of roots, guarantees that a thermometer passes through every intermediate temperature, and underlies the bisection method.

title: The Cantor Set
subject: Real Analysis
statement: There is a subset of [0,1] that is uncountable, has Lebesgue measure zero, and contains no interval.
short: Remove the middle third repeatedly: what remains has as many points as the original interval but zero length.
long: The Cantor set is closed, perfect and nowhere dense. Its points correspond bijectively to infinite sequences of 0s and 2s in ternary expansion, which makes it uncountable. Yet the total length removed is 1, so the leftover measure is zero. It is a standard counterexample to the intuition that large cardinality implies positive size.
proof: After n steps the remaining set has 2^n intervals of length 3^{-n}, so its measure is (2/3)^n \to 0. Ternary expansions using only digits 0 and 2 give a surjection from {0,2}^N onto C.
consequence: It motivates fractal dimension, supplies pathological measures, and shows that a continuous function can map a measure-zero set onto an interval (via the Cantor function).

title: Non-Measurable Sets Exist
subject: Real Analysis
statement: Assuming the axiom of choice, there is a set of real numbers that has no Lebesgue measure.
short: The Vitali set breaks translation-invariance: assigning it any measure leads to a contradiction.
long: Choose one representative from each equivalence class of reals modulo the rationals inside [0,1]. The translates of this Vitali set by rationals are pairwise disjoint and cover [0,1]. If the set had positive measure, countably many disjoint translates would have infinite total measure inside a finite interval; if it had zero measure, their union would have measure zero instead of one.
proof: Lebesgue measure is countably additive and translation invariant. The disjoint rational translates sum to either 0 or \infty, but they cover [0,1], whose measure is 1 — a contradiction.
consequence: It explains why measure theory restricts itself to sigma-algebras and why the axiom of choice has genuinely non-constructive consequences.

title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
subject: Real Analysis
statement: Differentiation and integration are inverse operations: the integral of a derivative recovers the net change.
short: The local rate of change accumulating over an interval gives exactly the global change.
long: The theorem has two parts. The first says that differentiating an accumulated-area function returns the original continuous integrand. The second says that any antiderivative can be used to evaluate a definite integral, turning an infinite limiting process into a finite computation.
proof: Partition [a,b] and sum f(x_i)-f(x_{i-1}) = f'(c_i)\Delta x_i using the mean value theorem; the right-hand sums converge to the integral.
consequence: It is the bridge between differential equations and integral equations, and the reason area, displacement and accumulated quantity share one formalism.

title: The Basel Problem
subject: Real Analysis
statement: The sum of the reciprocals of the squares of the positive integers equals pi squared over six.
short: A purely arithmetic series unexpectedly evaluates to a transcendental constant.
long: Euler evaluated this sum in 1734, connecting number theory with analysis. His argument factored the infinite product for sin(x)/x and compared the coefficient of x squared with its Taylor expansion — a step whose rigour was clarified much later by the Weierstrass factorisation theorem.
proof: sin x / x = \prod_{n\ge1}(1-x^2/(n^2\pi^2)); expanding the x^2 coefficient gives -\sum 1/(n^2\pi^2), which must equal -1/6.
consequence: It opened the door to the Riemann zeta function, whose values at even integers are all rational multiples of powers of pi.

title: The Gaussian Integral
subject: Real Analysis
statement: The bell curve has total area exactly the square root of pi.
short: A trick in two dimensions evaluates an integral that has no elementary antiderivative.
long: Squaring the integral and switching to polar coordinates converts an intractable one-dimensional problem into a simple radial one. This is one of the classic examples where changing the dimension makes the calculation easier.
proof: Let I be the integral. Then I^2=\iint e^{-(x^2+y^2)}dx\,dy = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}r\,dr\,d\theta = \pi.
consequence: It fixes the normalising constant of the normal distribution and appears throughout probability, statistics and quantum mechanics.

title: The Mean Value Theorem
subject: Real Analysis
statement: A differentiable function has a point where its instantaneous slope equals its average slope over an interval.
short: Somewhere on the trip your speedometer read exactly your average speed.
long: The theorem requires continuity on the closed interval and differentiability on the open interval. It is the key step in proving that a function with zero derivative is constant, and in estimating how much a function can change.
proof: Apply Rolle's theorem to f(x) minus the line through (a,f(a)) and (b,f(b)); the auxiliary function has equal endpoint values and vanishes derivative at an interior maximum or minimum.
consequence: It yields bounds on approximation error, Lipschitz estimates, and the standard proof that antiderivatives differ by a constant.

title: Pointwise Is Not Uniform Convergence
subject: Real Analysis
statement: A sequence of continuous functions can converge pointwise to a discontinuous limit.
short: Every x^n is smooth, but the limit jumps at the endpoint — so the convergence cannot be uniform.
long: For each fixed x below 1 the powers tend to zero, while at x=1 they stay at one. The limit function is discontinuous, which is impossible under uniform convergence. The speed of convergence slows down arbitrarily as x approaches 1.
proof: Uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous; the pointwise limit above is not, hence convergence is not uniform. Equivalently sup|x^n-f| = 1 for every n.
consequence: It motivates uniform convergence as the hypothesis needed to exchange limits with continuity, integration and differentiation.

title: The Weierstrass Function
subject: Real Analysis
statement: There is a function continuous everywhere and differentiable nowhere.
short: Infinitely many corners survive every magnification: continuity does not imply smoothness.
long: Nineteenth-century intuition held that a continuous function should be differentiable except at isolated points. Weierstrass disproved this with a uniformly convergent sum of ever-faster cosine waves. Its graph is a fractal: no matter how far you zoom in, no straightening occurs.
proof: Uniform convergence gives continuity. Difference quotients at carefully chosen scales blow up because the high-frequency terms dominate when ab is large enough.
consequence: It forced a rigorous separation between continuity and differentiability and helped originate fractal geometry.

title: Dominated Convergence
subject: Real Analysis
statement: A dominated sequence of measurable functions may be integrated by taking the limit inside the integral.
latex: |f_n|\le g\in L^1,\ f_n\to f\ \text{a.e.}\Longrightarrow \lim_n\int f_n=\int f
short: An integrable ceiling is exactly what is needed to move a limit past an integral sign.
long: Pointwise convergence alone is not enough: mass can escape to infinity. If all functions are bounded in absolute value by a single integrable function, Fatou's lemma applied to 2g-|f_n-f| gives the result and rules out escaping mass.
proof: Apply Fatou's lemma to g+f_n and g-f_n, then combine the two inequalities to get equality of the limits.
consequence: It is the standard tool for differentiating under the integral sign and for interchanging limits in Fourier analysis and probability.

title: Taylor's Theorem with Remainder
subject: Real Analysis
statement: A smooth function is a polynomial plus a controlled error term.
short: Local derivative data approximates the function, and the remainder tells you how wrong you are.
long: The Lagrange form of the remainder involves a derivative at some unknown intermediate point. This is enough to prove that analytic functions equal their Taylor series and to bound truncation errors in numerical algorithms.
proof: Repeated integration by parts, or a generalised Cauchy mean value theorem, gives R_n(x)=f^{(n+1)}(\xi)(x-a)^{n+1}/(n+1)! for some \xi between a and x.
consequence: It underlies numerical approximation, asymptotic analysis, and the error estimates for Newton's method.

title: The Riemann–Lebesgue Lemma
subject: Real Analysis
statement: The Fourier coefficients of an integrable function tend to zero at high frequency.
short: Rapid oscillation cancels out: no integrable signal has a persistent high-frequency component.
long: The lemma is the analytic reason Fourier series converge in a meaningful averaged sense and why spectra of reasonable signals decay. It relies on approximating an integrable function by step functions, for which the cancellation is immediate.
proof: The claim is easy for indicator functions of intervals, hence for step functions; density of step functions in L^1 and boundedness of the Fourier transform extend it to all integrable functions.
consequence: It is a prerequisite for the Riemann localisation principle and for convergence results in harmonic analysis.

title: Brouwer's Fixed-Point Theorem
subject: Real Analysis
statement: Every continuous map from a closed ball to itself has a fixed point.
short: Stir a cup of coffee and some point ends up exactly where it started.
long: The result fails for an open disc (a small rotation has no fixed point) and for a punctured disc, so compactness and the absence of holes are essential. In dimension one it is just the intermediate value theorem.
proof: Sperner's lemma applied to finer triangulations, or equivalently the non-retractability of the ball onto its boundary, yields the fixed point in the limit.
consequence: It proves Nash equilibrium existence, solutions to certain games and economic models, and is a gateway to algebraic topology.

title: The Dirichlet Function
subject: Real Analysis
statement: The indicator of the rationals is discontinuous everywhere, yet Lebesgue integrable with integral zero.
short: Rationals and irrationals are both dense, so the function oscillates at every scale — but the rationals are a null set.
long: Every interval contains rational and irrational numbers, so no point has a limit. Riemann's integral cannot handle it, while Lebesgue's integral can because the set where the function is nonzero has measure zero. It cleanly separates two notions of integration.
proof: Density gives discontinuity at every point. The rationals are countable, hence of measure zero, so the Lebesgue integral of their indicator is zero.
consequence: It illustrates why Lebesgue integration extends Riemann integration and why almost-everywhere statements are powerful.
